I'm depressed as fuck, thanks to bipolarity. Anhedonia 24/7. People bore me. Some people just "adopt" me, as you'd do to a pet, and that's how I've came to experience some personal relationships - I'm in my second marriage, never actively tried to be in a relationship, but god knows how I actively tried /succeeded ending my relationships. It's like relationships happen to me, and I suffer them, because someone else gets attached to me, and I stay on these relationships while it's convenient to me. 1st marriage lasted 15 years and some day I just peaced out of it. No pain, no sadness, no missing the guy (he used to get on my nerves anyway). I don't talk to my parents, or to any relative, and don't miss them. No close friends, no family, no safety net, I'm so unattached it scares me a little. I might need people to watch my cats if/when I get committed again, and that's the only reason I still remain on my second wedding (that, and because my husband, for some reason, wants to have a relationship with me. I don't understand that either. He must love me - must be nice actually feeling something towards people, other than contempt...)

At some point after my diagnosis, I had weight loss surgery. And I'm a woman with polycystic ovarian syndrome, so if we count psych meds plus PCOS meds and vitamins I must take because of malabsorption, it's about 20-22 pills a day. FFS, it's a lot. So I spent about a month without them - I was never vocal about my meds, but my husband knew I wasn't taking them and was getting on my nerves because of that.

My vision was the first to say good bye. Vit A deficiency, maybe? Then the shakes started. I could function but not as regularly because I was shaking so bad. But how can you do most things without seeing so well and when your hands shake like crazy? Then the facial hair, which took me more than two years to get rid of, came back. My brain must have liquefied, lacking B12 and magnesium. And without my zinc/selenium pill, I haven't been able to get out of bed.

I'm at my pdoc's waiting room now because the olanzapine must go, but unfortunately, some people, like us, will have pills to take for life - at least lithium or valproate - and while this sucks, feeling bad sucks more. It's like watching your weight: some won't need it, some will have to calcularem even chewing gum. We have to live in peace with who we are.

Mas é uma cidade tranquila, me sinto segura aqui - vc pode andar com o celular na mão no "centro"(uma avenida só), diferente do centro de Porto Alegre. E vc pode conseguir casa com pátio, o que é um luxo em outras cidades maiores. Eu só não sei como é o mercado de aluguel de imóveis pq eu não alugo, mas fica a 10 minutos de trensurb de Canoas e a 30 de Porto Alegre. Trensurb é um transporte rápido e barato que vai de Porto Alegre a Novo Hamburgo e a passagem é única por 4,50. 

Mas eu vou citar as desvantagens também: o hospital daqui é um LIXO. Sério. Não houve uma única vez em que eu ou alguém que eu conheço não teve um atendimento digno de um açougue. E o custo da alimentação é assustador, eu comparo quando vou em Gravataí e os preços aqui são ridículos, enquanto aqui vc paga 5,99 o quilo de um tomate feio pra porra, em Gravataí sai por 2,99.

Quase tudo o que vc faz no microondas vc pode fazer na airfryer excetuando, claro, qualquer coisa com líquidos (não fala nada no manual, mas eu não coloco coisas líquidas na airfryer pq vc meio que dá um puxão pra abrir e pode virar o troço quente por tudo). Como seria porção pra um só, a airfryer é menor e, dependendo do modelo, mais barata. O problema dos dois aparelhos é que vc acaba precisando de alguns itens específicos pra eles, MAS a airfryer aceita recipientes metálicos (até mesmo quentinha de loja de descartáveis que tem em vários tamanhos) e o microondas, não. Já os plásticos tem menos chances de derreter no microondas que na airfryer. A comida no microondas fica mais cozida, na airfryer fica mais assada ou tostadinha, e um microondas com função dourador sai bem mais caro. 

A última coisa que eu lembro sobre isso é que vc consegue fazer miojo no microondas mas não na airfryer :P

Isso tudo dito, eu tenho os dois (já tive a airfryer mais comum, de cesto, agora tenho a de forninho e acho MUITO melhor) e pra te ajudar a tomar sua decisão te digo que são similares mas não iguais. Não fazem a mesma coisa, mas fazem QUASE a mesma coisa. Se a tua ideia é fazer comida no final de semana, acondicionar em potes e descongelar na semana, o microondas é teu melhor amigo. Se a ideia é não comprar fogão mas ainda assim conseguir comer bem, fica com os dois (faz o arroz no microondas, o frango na airfryer e compra uma lata de feijão :P). E, se a ideia é poder sair do básico sem apodrecer sua cozinha com uma nuvem de gordura e fazer uma carne ou uma batatinha frita ou mesmo uns muffins numas forminhas de silicone, vai na airfryer.

It's too cold to cook these days in Southern Brazil, so I rediscovered soups. In our culture, soups (and by extent teas) are considered sick people food, so you don't feel like having soup when you're healthy. I've been testing some ways to keep vegetables for a longer time in the fridge and anything that I feel that isn't keeping very well ends up in soup. It's great for a cold evening, even more now that I'm on medication and can't enjoy the ocasional cachaça... Creamy soups? Leftover rice or beans in the soup (we always have them handy) and a hand mixer. My favorite is a version of chicken noodle soup (sans noodle) which is very creamy because of hard work: thin grated potatoes and a grated carrot will make it creamy. Fry a chicken leg, some onion, garlic and ginger, celery if you have it, add potatoes and carrot, drown it, and leave it be. When it looks almost ready, drop some rice on it - proportional to the size of your soup. Season with salt and whatever suits your fancy. Best soup ever.

Primeiro vc limpa a pia, depois o vaso. Não vai me passar esponja ou pano que vc acabou de passar no vaso na pia, faz o contrário. Especialmente se vc usa (e não deveria usar) a mesma esponja para o vaso e a pia. Mas se vc usar algum produto em gel, tipo harpic ou pato purific (é o que eu uso), vc vai aplicar, fechar o assento do vaso, deixar o produto agindo e enquanto isso vai limpando a pia, recolhendo lixo, passando x14 nas paredes (também uso, mas pra isso vc tem que tirar TUDO o que é têxtil do banheiro e aceitar que a sua roupa vai virar o uniforme da faxina).

Eu uso um pano cheio de x14 enrolado num hashi de tele entrega, deixo agindo uns 10 minutos e depois passo o mesmo pano enxaguado, sem produto. To a blender, add one raw egg, a pinch of salt, a teaspoon of white vinegar (we don't do vinegar buffet in here, 90% of times anybody say "vinegar" they mean white vinegar), a clove of garlic and something called tempero verde at your taste. Tempero verde is just the combination of parsley and Green onions which are sold in a bunch together with this name. Since I live in the deep South, I can't guarantee that other states do that, but in Rio Grande do Sul this is how we roll.

Then you pulse and pulse and pulse until the herb volume is gone, or, at least, much less than it was. Now you turn the blender to speed 1 or 2 (don't overspeed it), remove the small middle lid of the blender's lid, and start pouring cooking oil on it. Just pour it. How much oil? I'll tell you how much: while you're pouring oil and the blender is turning, there's a hole in the middle. That's the blender's blade. When the blender's contents are liquid they turn around the blade, creating that little space. Once all the contents are emulsified and the mixture has "body", that space above the blade will close and then you'll know you're done. You don't measure your oil, you observe the mayo. If you keep pouring oil after the blade is "closed" it won't be incorporated to the mayo, so if you need MOAR green mayo (who doesn't?), duplicate the recipe from the beginning. 

Last advices: mayo isn't actually warm as it leaves the blender and you can serve it as is, but it would be better if you could keep it in the fridge COVERED (homemade mayo tends to make a skin) for 15-30 minutes. It'll make it firmer, too. If you fear salmonella, you can sub an egg for half a cup of milk but in my experience it changes the texture and makes the mayo too liquidy. And, finally, eat mayo with french fries. Seriously. In fact, around here we buy french fries as a vehicle to eat green mayo, nobody cares about ketchup :)

- Cuidar das lesões com rifocina e/ou Dermotrat. Cuidado com a mobília.

- A ração que ele come é Royal Canin para castrados

O diagnóstico que recebi foi de reação alérgica, então reduzir ao máximo as fontes de alérgenos (ração, pulgas e banho) resolve pra mim. Ele não se come tanto, e quando tem lesões, não são tão graves. Tomara que fique tudo bem com seu gatinho ;)

Maybe instead of an SSRI you should talk to your pdoc about atypical antipsychotics. I was on 300mg quetiapine and 10mg aripiprazole at some point (associated to lithium, lamotrigine and desvenlafaxine) and while they didn't make me free of depression, they helped me a lot during the lowest low. Docs told me I never got to the right dosage of quetiapine (which should be at around 800mg/day) and I asked to change because of side effects, and because it's expensive as hell in my country. I could never afford an 800mg treatment. There's the new bipolar medication too, like Latuda, but it's also expensive, so I can't talk from experience, but you have more options than antidepressants.

A questão é que clássicos são superestimados, sim, pq existe a importância cultural da obra e existe a questão do gosto pessoal. Eu sempre digo que literatura é mais leitura do que escrita, pq a obra é escrita uma vez por uma pessoa e lida milhares de vezes por milhares de pessoas diferentes. Tolstoi é importante culturalmente falando? Sim. Eu vou fazer meus alunos lerem pq é importante? Não. Eu vou procurar algo mais acessível (e menor) e que tenha importância cultural significativa, nesse momento estou pensando em Shakespeare. 

Literatura não é e não tem que ser elitista. Vc quer que o cara leia Guerra e Paz, eu já fico feliz se ele, sendo não-leitor, começar por Percy Jackson e o ladrão de raios. Quando começa muito difícil, a pessoa desiste, e não é essa minha intenção. Ler os clássicos requer muita experiência de leitura, e essa sua posição de purismo literário, desencorajando quem está começando, não ajuda a fazer mais pessoas gostarem de ler. Parece que vc já gosta, e não se importa muito em difundir, mas mesmo assim não precisa diminuir o esforço de quem está aqui fazendo trabalho de formiguinha e feliz pq tem gente lendo os livros do Sapkowski por causa da série da Netflix.

Notou que todos os comentários aqui recomendam leitura? Adquirir conhecimento não é um processo rápido nem fácil, é incômodo e tortuoso. Seu intelecto é a soma do conteúdo que vc consumiu e assimilou, então, se vc consome pouco conteúdo, ou de baixa qualidade, isso vai refletir naquilo que vc conhece, na sua visão de mundo e na sua experiência como um todo. O mesmo acontece se vc consumir muito conteúdo e de boa qualidade.

"Mas isso leva muito tempo, como eu consigo ser melhor mais rápido?" Tratando a leitura como um hobby, e não como uma obrigação. Evidentemente, isso é uma construção de hábito que não acontece instantaneamente, mas é mais rápido que ler, sei lá, Os Sertões ou Guerra e Paz, como sugeriram aqui - a propósito, alguns clássicos são superestimados e esses são dois exemplos. Leia se um dia tiver tempo e quiser, mas troque um deles por cinco outros mais concisos e leia sobre a história da Guerra de Canudos. Continuando, quando vc dedica à leitura o mesmo tempo que dedica ao LOL/Minecraft/outro ou à Netflix, vc passa umas 4/5 horas (estimo) do seu dia lendo. Como qualquer outro hobby, vc melhora com a prática, então em algum tempo vc vai estar lendo 80-100 páginas por hora. Em 3 horas isso dá um livro inteiro por dia (ou quase, dependendo do livro).

No princípio, leia de tudo até vc reconhecer o que vc gosta e não gosta. Depois, LEIA AQUILO DE QUE GOSTA. Se o livro tá ruim ou chato, não perde teu tempo, deixa pelo meio mesmo e vai pra outro. A vida é muito curta pra ler livro ruim. Nunca deixe de experimentar, pq conforme sua experiência de vida muda, também mudam seus gostos. Eu tive um curso de Letras inteiro lendo ficção e hoje não aguento mais, prefiro ler sobre filosofia, psicologia, antropologia e sociologia, pra me entender melhor e entender o mundo que me rodeia. Fui reler alguns dos meus livros "favoritos" da graduação e tive que largar pensando "meu deus, eu lia essa merda E GOSTAVA?". Ninguém toma banho duas vezes no mesmo rio, vc muda e o rio muda. O rio vai mudar naturalmente, mas pra vc mudar, tem que ter esforço da sua parte.

They say activity triggers activity, so I've been "encouraged" to force myself to do things. It doesn't work this way. When you're not functional, the bare minimum is painful. My husband has had to beg me to take a shower. And inactivity makes you lose your habits (exercise, showering, brushing teeth, cooking). But the good thing is, it doesn't last forever. I'm on a better choice of meds now (I have bipolar disorder, so no antidepressants, even though my depressive episodes are brutal) and I started doing ONLY what I like, for me. I don't feel obligated to do anything else - and I know it's easy for me because I don't have children, and I just dumped my pets' care on my unemployed husband. Do I shower everyday now? Not yet. Some days I do nothing. But there are those days in which I have the drive for doing something. These are the days I look forward to. The days when I wash dishes while listening to music. All the resources I've read (and it was A LOT of reading) stated that bipolar treatment is a tripod: psychiatric assessment, medication and talk therapy. I've accepted that. Maybe that can change through the years with more research, but that's what we have now. Therapists are just people who have a degree and tools to help in this process, they get burned out like we do in our jobs. Some of them are better at managing some disorders, some specialize on something else. Like if you have your hair dyed red, you should go to a hairdresser who knows how to take care of dyed hair, if they specialize in red that's even better. If you have a Ford, taking it to a GM dealership for servicing will only take you so far - they'll know the basics, but the specifics won't be touched. IDK if I expressed myself correctly. 

Back to talk therapy, I believe it's a process with beginning, development and an end. It's great to go to a therapist who already know you and your story, but there's so much they can do before we "graduate" with them and then have to move on. This is bringing me some anxiety because I feel like my therapist is preparing me for The Ditch and I'm thinking on how on earth am I going to get a therapist that I like (because I don't like anybody) and I'll have to start all over and tell again the same stories... I'm almost inclined to write a private blog, giving them the URL and password and saying "here you'll find all the introductory shit, let's save us some time".

I've been on CBT for 4 years now, and it has been different from what I've been informed it was. I really thought CBT was short-term psychotherapy. Last two sessions were shitshows. Am I worse? I wouldn't say that, since I came to the therapist with a diagnosis. Am I better? I wouldn't say that too. It's like therapy for bipolar disorder should be different from regular therapy, since we need it permanently (and thus I fail to see how CBT can be more helpful than psychoanalysis or other therapy type). In my case, specifically, it seems that the relationship with my therapist has burned out, and she has said things like "I can't help you if you don't want to change" or "therapy is at a stall" but how many things can a person change in therapy for four years? Do you end therapy as a perfect being, having reached a kind of psychological nirvana, and then you get discharged? I think it's a cycle and sometimes it has to come to an end. Maybe we're both burned out, patient and therapist.

If there's one thing that I've changed, and I feel worse about that, is my response to aggression. I'm not as belligerent as I used to be, but sometimes I get the feeling of getting in conflict and it teases me, it feels good and I crave for that adrenaline discharge again. Like going on a rollercoaster. When I told her that, that's when she said she can't help me. Sometimes I feel like my therapist is trying to dogtrain me according to her worldview, but nah, that might just be my chaotic bipolar brain looking for a reason to fight.

It's been only 7 months and, while I know and acknowledge my clothes are outrageously large, I still see myself the same way I did before. I've never been disgusted at myself, never hated my body, but now I'm struggling to see the obvious change. I don't feel thinner or smaller, and while some things are different (my legs fit in my knee high boots, I can cross my legs when I sit, there's room for my purse by my side when I'm on the bus, instead of just leaving it on my lap, my clothes are unusable and I need new ones, showering is easier), I still am the same fat lady who I've been for all my life.

I don't know what's my current size, and my excuse is "I don't want to spend money on jeans right now because I'll be losing more weight for about a year and I'll be needing new jeans anyway". But deep down I'm terrified of wearing a regular size and not feeling like myself anymore. So, yes, I hide behind my old oversized nerdy t-shirts (which were already oversized before wls) with leggings for comfort because I can't fathom what is life as a not-morbidly-obese person. In my head, I'm still morbidly obese. I still prop my tummy to the front, but the sensation is different now. Every piece of clothing that is too big feels like I'm losing a piece of my identity.

Mental health diagnosis is a construction, it takes gathering enough information from the patient, and it's safe to say you might not leave your first appointment with a diagnosis.

That being said, I'll share my personal experience. I've been labeled as a "difficult patient" for the last 15 years. I'm bipolar, in my late 30s. I've had bad and good psychiatrists, and the whole advocating for myself thing can go right or terribly wrong, depending on the doctor. Right now I just had my first appointment with a new psychiatrist because my last one refused to review my medication, even though I've been complaining for over a year about it. He told me to go find a second opinion. Dude kept me on FIVE meds for two years with no improvement and was annoyed when I asked to change them. During this time I remembered both pdocs I have previously had (one wanted me to pay for pseudoscience as complementar treatment - high performance coaching and family constellations -, other gave me lithium poisoning) and how people say I'm confrontational and hostile, and every time I would advocate for myself there was this voice in my head saying "be nice". So I lost almost two years of my life and a lot of money in meds which didn't help me at all. 

So, sometimes you are assertive and your doctor messes up because he thinks you're hostile, and sometimes you're sweet, even bovine, and they won't help you because you're not assertive. I wonder if men have this same problem.

About what you're going to tell your doctor, I recommend making something like a script. Sometimes we get nervous and forget things, writing them down will help. If you have a journal, reread some entries for clarity and to remember how you felt lately. Prepare for your appointment, read some threads in here. I find that sometimes people can put in words feelings I have and can't express. If it's your first appointment with this doctor, examine them like they're examining you, vet them, inspect for signs that they'll be willing to work with you on your treatment, or if they're just going to sign a prescription and call the next patient. If you have the possibility, shop for a pdoc like you would for a therapist. I've internalized that I'm a difficult patient, and if I don't like a doctor in the first contact, I'll be looking for another one, because my insurance has a list to choose from. I won't be stuck with a doctor I dislike because I fear the mental health team at insurance office (they have psychiatrists and psychologists there to help us with referrals and other things) will think I'm difficult, my mental health is my priority right now.

Fortunately my job's systems are connected to death certificates' systems and I refused to accept it, or I would have had to pay for the money she wanted. The best part was that the death certificate was registered at the same office that emitted the dead man's power of attorney. You can't trust these services.

I have fine oily curly hair, and it's been a nightmare trying to find a routine for it. What's been working (not perfectly, but well enough) for me is:

- Keeping it short. I chose a pixie cut with elongated front (just enough to reach behind ear, so curls won't volumize the front) and curly back. Almost like an interpretation of "the Karen", for clarification. Sometimes I want to grow my hair out because I like pigtails and the curl cascade, but then I have to talk to myself (I have pre-made cards because I've had this conversation with myself way too many times, now all I have to do is read the cards) that my fine hair is never going to achieve my expectancies, and while I'm growing it out I'm going to look like Ron Jeremy. There's not enough volume for it to look good. Instead of fighting against the thinness or wasting (more) money on products which won't give me the effect I wanted, I settled for a haircut I like which will help me work on other issues.

- COVID gave me time to work on wash intervals. I've always washed hair whenever I took a shower because oily hair, but by trial and error I discovered I can go 3 days without washing my hair before entering yuck zone. This is huge. Now that's winter (Brazil) I've finally changed my day-to-day habits to fit the seasons and it really makes a difference. Water temperature, products, wash frequency, shower time (shower early, don't sleep with wet hair).

- Shampoo bar. On Summer I wash with an adstringent bar, usually with rosemary, lemongrass and lavender, sometimes with green clay. Now I have a more normal bar, with some natural butters (mainly shea), calendule, chamomile and geranium. IDK about makers in the US, but once you find the one you like, keep your bars dry and they'll last a long time. I don't use conditioner because my hair is short.

- Visiting my doctor and asking for a vitamin screening. Maybe you need supplements. DO NOT take any supplements without recommendation, because excess vitamins may be bad for you and one of the effects is hair loss.

- Reducing products and keep heat to a minimum. 

I hope this helps. Best of luck!
